title: A second stress fracture and no period
objective: Explain the female athlete triad as low energy availability (intake that falls short of what training burns, with or without an eating disorder) combined with menstrual disorder and reduced bone mineral density
secondaryObjectives: Recognize stress fractures as overload injuries, 0.7% to 20% of sports medicine clinic injuries; flag high-risk sites (femoral neck, anterior tibia, tarsal navicular, talus, sesamoids, 5th metatarsal) where non-union risk is high

brief.situation: 15:30 in a sports physical therapy clinic. You are the physical therapist. Maya, 17, a cross-country runner, is back for her return-to-run plan after a tibial stress fracture, her second stress fracture this year. Her coach has emailed asking you to 'get her to 50 miles a week for the season'. Her mother is with her.
handover: Her imaging report shows the tibial fracture healing; her pain is gone with walking.
Clinic policy: for a minor, share concerns with the parent present; refer suspected energy or eating problems to the team physician the same day.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: More load on unready bone raises the fracture risk. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

why.question: Why has Maya had two stress fractures, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Possible female athlete triad: low energy availability (skipped meals, weight loss, worry about racing weight), a menstrual disorder (7 months without a period) and likely reduced bone density, shown by two stress fractures; the summer mileage spike added load.
parts.modelAnswer: Probably the triad. She's not eating enough for her training, hasn't had a period in 7 months, and two stress fractures suggest weak bones. The mileage jump made it worse.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Hold running at a low level, explain to her and her mother, refer to the team physician today for evaluation and bone density with dietitian and mental health support, and tell the coach only that she is on a held plan.
parts.modelAnswer: Keep her at walk-run, explain it to her and her mom, and call the team doctor today for a workup, a dietitian and a counselor.

scoring.modelReasoning: The female athlete triad is low energy availability (intake short of what training burns, with or without an eating disorder) combined with menstrual disorder and reduced bone mineral density. Two stress fractures in a year with 7 months of no periods and restricted eating fits it. Hold the load, explain, and refer to the team physician the same day; the femoral neck is a high-risk stress fracture site.
